subject: sg-succession
note:
Sweep over FOUR Singapore Acts — the Wills Act 1838, the Intestate Succession Act 1967, the Probate and Administration Act 1934 and the Guardianship of Infants Act 1934. SUPERSEDES jl4/examples/legal/sg-succession/denovo/external-modifications.json, which covered three of them as swept on 18 Aug 2026; that file is left on disk as the record of what was deposited then and is no longer declared by the subject. Sixty searches and forty-eight raw findings; every finding was independently corroborated, and where the corroboration corrected the finding it is the corrected version that is recorded here.

DISPOSITIONS WERE WRITTEN BEFORE THE ENCODING WAS READABLE. The L4 encoding of this subject was being written while this register was assembled, so no entry is disposed `encoded`: doing so would assert a fact about a file this sweep did not read. `deferred` says what would have to be true instead. Whoever finishes the encoding should re-read the deferred entries against it and promote the ones it actually reflects.

THERE IS NO FORK REGISTER FOR THIS ENCODING YET, so every entry's routing.fork_ids is the empty array — written rather than omitted, because an empty array is an answer. That has one visible consequence: the schema requires an interpretive entry disposed `encoded` or `deferred` to name the fork it opens or settles, so no interpretive entry in this register can be disposed `deferred` even where `deferred` is what it deserves. Those entries are disposed `subsumed` and their notes say plainly that the construction is not known to be reflected in the encoding and must be — E18 (ISA s 7 Rule 9 read down) and E19 (PAA s 18 priority following ISA s 7) are the two to read first. Read the notes, not the enum.

SSO exposes a per-Act version timeline rather than the UK-style F-marker apparatus, so the annotation inventory in the source bundle is the set of superseded dated versions and the dispositions below join on it.

THE LIVE AMBIGUITY AT THE CENTRE OF THIS ENCODING is the age of an "infant" under the Guardianship of Infants Act — E1 to E4. The Act defines only "court" and never defines "infant"; neither the Interpretation Act 1965 nor the Civil Law Act 1909 supplies a general age of majority, and CLA s 35 is confined to contracts with s 35(3)(b) expressly preserving age requirements stated in other written laws. The number 21 is stated by a rule of court, by an obiter parenthesis in a forum non conveniens judgment, and by an undated web page — three institutional layers, no statute among them.

searches.question: Has any Singapore court construed GIA s 3's "welfare of the infant is the first and paramount consideration"?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `judgments` corpus (Singapore judgments: SGCA, SGHC(A), SGHC, SGHCF, SGHCR, SGFC), full-text relevance search, run 2026-08-26. 20 results reviewed; 6 judgments opened in full.
searches.query: Guardianship of Infants Act section 3 welfare of the infant first and paramount consideration
searches.coverage_note: Does NOT cover: unreported/unwritten decisions (most GIA custody work is oral, at Family Court level, and never produces a written GD); Syariah Court decisions, which are not in this corpus at all and which decide custody for Muslim parties; anything decided after the corpus's last ingest, which I did not independently verify — the newest hit was [2026] SGFC 40 (23 Mar 2026), so the corpus is silent on Apr–Aug 2026 and I cannot tell whether that is because nothing was decided or because nothing was ingested. Relevance ranking, not exhaustive enumeration: I did not page past the first 20 hits, so a low-ranked but important case could have been missed.

searches.question: Has any Singapore court construed ISA s 3's definition of "child" — the position of illegitimate and adopted children on intestacy?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `judgments` corpus, full-text search, run 2026-08-26. 6 results, all reviewed; 2 opened in full (AAG v Estate of AAH; Lim Weipin).
searches.query: Intestate Succession Act section 3 definition of child legitimate illegitimate adopted intestacy
searches.coverage_note: Only 6 hits total, which is itself suspicious for a query this central — the corpus may index ISA cases thinly, or the phrasing may have been too narrow. I did NOT run the complementary searches that would test that: nothing on "Adoption of Children Act 2022" and its effect on the ISA definition, nothing on legitimation under the Legitimacy Act 1934 s 3, and nothing on foreign adoption orders. Does not cover academic commentary, Law Reform Committee reports, or MinLaw consultation papers, any of which could signal impending change to a definition that has been criticised for decades.

searches.question: Has any Singapore court construed ISA s 7's distribution rules or the per stirpes division in Rule 3?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `judgments` corpus, run 2026-08-26. 5 results, all reviewed; 3 opened (Cheng Tze Tzuen, Wong Swee Hor, Lim Weipin).
searches.query: Intestate Succession Act section 7 rule 3 per stirpes distribution surviving spouse issue
searches.coverage_note: Five hits for the operative distribution provision of the Act is thin coverage, and I did not run separate searches per Rule — Rules 5, 6, 7 and 8 (parents, siblings, grandparents, uncles/aunts) were never searched individually and are effectively unswept. I found the Rule 9 read-down only incidentally, inside a case retrieved for a different reason, which is direct evidence that provision-by-provision searching would have found more. Does not cover the arithmetic of per stirpes as applied in unreported distribution orders.

searches.question: Has any Singapore court construed ISA s 2's exclusion of Muslims, or drawn the boundary with the Syariah Court?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `judgments` corpus, run 2026-08-26. 7 results reviewed; Shafeeg (CA) opened in full across two offset fetches.
searches.query: Intestate Succession Act section 2 does not apply to estate of any Muslim Syariah Court jurisdiction
searches.coverage_note: Does NOT cover Syariah Court judgments or MUIS fatwas, neither of which is in this corpus — and the boundary is precisely where those matter. Shafeeg CA itself shows the gap: the court had to reason about fatwas 20 and 41 from secondary description. I also did not search for the converse case (a non-Muslim estate with Muslim claimants, or a deceased whose Muslim status was disputed), nor for the domicile mismatch between ISA s 2 ("any Muslim", no domicile qualifier) and AMLA s 112(1) ("Muslim person domiciled in Singapore") — that gap is visible on the face of the two texts and I found no case resolving it, but I did not search for one.

searches.question: Has any Singapore court construed Wills Act s 6 (formal validity / mode of execution)?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `judgments` corpus, two queries run 2026-08-26; 24 results reviewed across both; Fauziyah v MUIS [2026] SGHC 104 opened in full.
searches.query: Wills Act section 6 formal validity signed at the foot or end attesting witnesses presence; and: will invalid not executed in accordance with section 6(2) Wills Act witnesses did not subscribe in presence of testator
searches.coverage_note: The first query returned heavily polluted results — the word "attest" pulled in criminal and disciplinary judgments — so ranking is unreliable here and I likely missed on-point cases below the noise. I did NOT open Lian Kok Hong v Lian Bee Leng [2015] SGHC 205 or Chai Choon Yong v CPF Board [2005] SGCA 13, both of which quote s 6(2) and either of which may contain a construction I have therefore not seen; I am reporting them as unexamined leads, not as findings. Nothing here covers s 6(3)–(4) (position of the signature) at all.

searches.question: Has any Singapore court construed Wills Act s 13 (revocation by marriage) or its "in contemplation of marriage" exception?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `judgments` corpus, three separate queries run 2026-08-26 with progressively looser phrasing, including a verbatim-text query on the words of s 13(1).
searches.query: Wills Act section 13 will revoked by marriage made in contemplation of marriage; Wills Act 1838 section 13 marriage revokes will exception power of appointment Intestate Succession Act 1967; every will made by a man or woman shall be revoked by his or her marriage
searches.coverage_note: NEGATIVE on the core question: the second query returned zero results, and no Singapore case was found that construes s 13 itself. What I found instead is adjacent — cases where s 13's automatic operation was the motive for attacking the marriage. So the honest statement is that s 13 appears judicially untouched in this corpus, not that it has been affirmed. I found NOTHING on s 13(2) — the "expressed to be made in contemplation of a marriage" exception, including its explicit polygamy clause — and nothing on how s 13 interacts with a marriage later declared void ab initio, which the 2025 conflict below makes live.

searches.question: Has any Singapore court construed PAA s 18(4)'s priority to letters of administration?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `judgments` corpus, run 2026-08-26. 4 results; Toh Seok Kheng and Cheng Tze Tzuen both opened in full.
searches.query: Probate and Administration Act section 18 letters of administration granted to husband widow next of kin discretion of court priority
searches.coverage_note: Four hits only. Does NOT cover the Family Justice (Probate and Other Matters) Rules 2024, which is where the operative priority order and the citation/renunciation machinery now actually live — Cheng Tze Tzuen points at P 6 rr 3, 38 and 39 of those Rules and I did not fetch or read them. Nor does it cover s 18(5) (estates of persons of a particular religion or race), s 18(3) (limited grants), or s 19 (attorney of an absent person). Contested grants are usually resolved without written grounds, so the written record understates the case law.

searches.question: Has any Singapore court construed PAA s 6(2)'s two-administrator rule where there is a minority or life interest?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `judgments` corpus, run 2026-08-26. 13 results reviewed; none opened in full because none disclosed a construction on the face of the snippet.
searches.query: Probate and Administration Act section 6(2) letters of administration minority life interest two administrators trust corporation
searches.coverage_note: NEGATIVE, with a caveat that matters: s 6(2) plainly IS being applied — [2025] SGFC 128 records a registry requirement for "the name of a co-administrator since there were minority interests", and [2009] SGHC 184 refers to "the costs and the delay in having a co-administrator". So the rule bites in practice while generating no reported construction. My negative therefore means "no court has read it down or glossed it", NOT "no court has engaged with it". I did not check the Family Justice (Probate and Other Matters) Rules 2024 or the FJC probate practice directions, which is where any operative gloss on s 6(2) would sit, and I did not open the two cases above to confirm what they say.

searches.question: Has any Singapore court construed GIA s 17's bar on a guardian giving a good discharge for a legacy?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `judgments` corpus, two independently-phrased queries run 2026-08-26 — one by section number and Act name, one by the operative statutory words with no Act name.
searches.query: Guardianship of Infants Act section 17 guardian good discharge legacy capital moneys payable to infant; and: guardian of the property of an infant good discharge legacy capital moneys court otherwise orders
searches.coverage_note: NEGATIVE and, I think, a real one: the first query returned zero results and the second returned two irrelevant trusts cases. Two differently-shaped queries both missing is better evidence than one. But the negative is only as good as the corpus — s 17 questions would typically be resolved by a registrar, a bank's or insurer's legal department, or the Public Trustee, none of which produce indexed judgments. So this is properly read as "no reported Singapore construction", not "no law". I did not check the Public Trustee's practice, the Trustees Act 1967 s 63 payment-into-court route, or CPF/insurance statutes that create their own discharge mechanisms for minors' money.

searches.question: Has any Singapore court construed GIA s 5's power to make custody and access orders?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `judgments` corpus, run 2026-08-26. 20 results reviewed; CX v CY, VET v VEU, UMF v UMG and UPD v UPC opened in full.
searches.query: section 5 Guardianship of Infants Act custody care and control joint custody order access
searches.coverage_note: This was the richest seam and I stopped at 20 results, so the tail is unexamined. Does NOT cover the very large body of Family Court decisions applying s 5 without construing it. Critically, it does not cover the overlap with the Women's Charter: most custody litigation in Singapore runs under WC ss 124–127 within divorce, not under the GIA, and I did not sweep the Women's Charter line at all — so a construction of "custody" laid down in a WC case and only later applied to the GIA would have been missed unless it happened to surface here.

searches.question: Has GIA s 5A (enforcement of child access orders, in force 2 Jan 2025) been judicially considered?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `judgments` corpus, run 2026-08-26.
searches.query: section 5A Guardianship of Infants Act enforcement of child access order breach compensate additional access bond
searches.coverage_note: NEGATIVE. One irrelevant hit. This is a weak negative and should be treated as such: s 5A commenced only on 2 January 2025, enforcement applications are made to a Family Court in a summons-like form under s 5A(7), and Family Court decisions rarely produce written grounds. Absence of reported authority ~19 months after commencement is expected, not informative. It does NOT establish that s 5A is inert. I did not check the Family Justice Rules made under s 5A(7)(b)(ii), which prescribe how such applications are actually dealt with and which are a live source of operative detail.

searches.question: Has any Singapore court construed GIA s 11 (matters to be considered: wishes of parent and infant), as amended with effect 31 Jan 2024?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `judgments` corpus, run 2026-08-26. 8 results reviewed; WKM v WKN [2024] SGCA 1 opened in full.
searches.query: section 11 Guardianship of Infants Act wishes of the parent wishes of the infant age to express independent opinion
searches.coverage_note: A trap I nearly fell into and am flagging rather than hiding: every substantive authority found here (ZO v ZP [2011], ATZ v AUA [2015], WKM v WKN [2024]) reasons from the PRE-amendment text of s 11, or from the parallel Women's Charter s 125(2)(b), not from the current s 11 as re-enacted by Act 18 of 2023 with effect 31 January 2024. WKM v WKN was decided 7 February 2024, one week after commencement, and quotes WC s 125(2)(b) rather than s 11. So the case law on this provision straddles a re-enactment and I found NO decision construing the current wording. Does not cover the Family Justice Reform Act 2023 parliamentary material that would explain what the re-enactment changed.

searches.question: Has any Singapore court construed the GIA's property-guardianship provisions (ss 15, 16, 18, 19, 20, 21)?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `judgments` corpus, run 2026-08-26.
searches.query: guardian of property of infant security section 15 16 18 19 sell mortgage lease permission of court infant estate
searches.coverage_note: NEGATIVE across the whole property half of the Act — one hit, and it was a custody case. Taken with the s 17 negative above, the picture is that GIA ss 15–21 are essentially judicially untouched in reported Singapore law. Caveats: this was a single broad query covering six sections at once rather than one query per section, which is exactly the shortcut I criticised in the ISA s 7 note above; a per-section sweep might do better. Also does not cover the Mental Capacity Act 2008 deputyship regime, which now absorbs much of the work these sections were written for, nor s 21's carve-out for money paid into a District Court, which is governed by Rules of Court I did not read.

searches.question: Has the GIA or ISA been challenged as unconstitutional under Art 12 (equality)?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `judgments` corpus, run 2026-08-26.
searches.query: Article 12 Constitution equality challenge Intestate Succession Act Guardianship of Infants Act unconstitutional discriminatory
searches.coverage_note: NEGATIVE — zero results. I place low confidence in this one. The query bundled a constitutional article, two Act names and three adjectives, which is a poor shape for a relevance search and may simply have matched nothing rather than found nothing. I know from Shafeeg (opened separately) that Art 12 arguments WERE canvassed at first instance about statutes that exclude Muslims, which means the zero-result is at least partly a query artefact. A proper sweep would search Art 12 jurisprudence directly and then check which statutes were challenged. Treat as unswept rather than clear.

searches.question: Is there any pending Bill amending the four Acts?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `bills` corpus, run 2026-08-26.
searches.query: Intestate Succession Act amendment Guardianship of Infants Act amendment Probate Administration Wills
searches.coverage_note: NEGATIVE, and explicitly outside this sweep's assigned lens (courts), included only because a pending Bill would be the single most consequential thing that could invalidate an encoding. Very low confidence: I do not know this corpus's coverage, currency or ingest cadence for Bills, I did not verify it against the Parliament website or the Government Gazette, and a single query returning zero from a corpus of unknown completeness is close to no evidence at all. Do not rely on this as clearance; P1 should own it.

searches.question: Has the pending appeal in Cheng Tze Tzuen v Dang Lan Anh been decided?
searches.scope: lawplain MCP `judgments` corpus, run 2026-08-26; plus a targeted fetch of [2026] SGHC(A) 2 to rule it out.
searches.query: Cheng Tze Tzuen Dang Lan Anh appeal marriage of convenience void intestate estate
searches.coverage_note: NEGATIVE — only the first-instance judgment is in the corpus, and [2026] SGHC(A) 2 turned out to be an unrelated matrimonial-assets appeal. This negative cannot distinguish "appeal not yet decided" from "decided but not yet ingested", and that distinction is the whole point. I did not check the Supreme Court hearing lists, the eLitigation docket, or SLW's judgment feed, any of which would settle it. Treat the conflict below as unresolved and re-check before relying on either side of it.

searches.question: Cross-check for very recent (2026) appellate decisions on any of the four Acts, using a second, independent method.
searches.scope: Two WebSearch queries run 2026-08-26 — one for 2026 SGCA decisions on the ISA/GIA, one for the status of the Cheng Tze Tzuen appeal.
searches.query: Singapore Court of Appeal 2026 "Intestate Succession Act" OR "Guardianship of Infants Act" judgment; and: "Cheng Tze Tzuen" appeal Singapore Appellate Division sham marriage estate 2026
searches.coverage_note: Weak as a cross-check and I want to be blunt about why: the tool's index is US-weighted and returned mostly law-firm marketing pages and links to the statutes themselves rather than judgments. Its one useful contribution was secondary — press reporting confirming the Cheng Tze Tzuen appeal was filed. It did NOT independently verify any pinpoint, and it is not a substitute for a docket check. So my "no 2026 appellate decision" conclusion rests on one corpus plus a poor second method, not on two good ones.

searches.question: Do the four Acts, as fetched, still match the versions in force — and what external statutes do they route to?
searches.scope: Read all four source .txt files plus AMLA1966.txt and CLA1909.txt at /Users/mengwong/src/legalese/l4wt/sg-family-gia/jl4/examples/legal/sg-succession/cleanroom-2026-08/source/, and fetch-manifest.json; grepped the informal-consolidation footers and searched each Act for "Muslim". Verified SCJA 1969 s 17A and the Legitimacy Act 1934's current status via the lawplain `statutes` corpus.
searches.query: grep 'version in force from' on each Act; grep -i 'muslim' on WA1838/PAA1934/GIA1934; lawplain statutes SCJA1969 s 17A; lawplain statutes Legitimacy Act
searches.coverage_note: Footers give WA 28/10/2022, PAA 15/10/2024, GIA 2/1/2025, and ISA no footer at all (so unchanged since the 2020 Rev Ed came into operation 31/12/2021); the manifest records all four as "Current version as at 25 Aug 2026". I verified currency only for SCJA s 17A and the Legitimacy Act — I did NOT re-verify AMLA s 111/s 112, Women's Charter s 5(2), or Family Justice Act 2014 s 22 against their current texts, and every one of those carries a finding below. AMLA's own footer reads 1/10/2025, later than three of the four subject Acts, which is a reminder that the satellite statutes move independently. Confirming a fetched text is current is P1's job; this is a spot-check, not clearance.

searches.question: What amendment trail do the four fetched PDFs carry on their face?
searches.scope: The four source .txt files in cleanroom-2026-08/source/
searches.query: grep -oE '\[Act [0-9]+ of [0-9]{4}[^]]*\]' WA1838.txt ISA1967.txt PAA1934.txt GIA1934.txt
searches.coverage_note: Reads only markers the Law Revision Commission chose to print. An amendment that is ENACTED BUT NOT COMMENCED leaves NO marker at all — this method is structurally blind to exactly the currency risk the lens asks about, which is why Finding 1 could not have been found this way and required the bill sweep instead. Also blind to amendments made by subsidiary legislation, and to savings provisions that live in the amending Act rather than the principal Act.

searches.question: What is each Act's 'Informal Consolidation – version in force from' date?
searches.scope: Four source .txt files
searches.query: grep -n 'Informal Consolidation' per file
searches.coverage_note: Establishes four DIFFERENT dates (WA 28/10/2022, PAA 15/10/2024, GIA 2/1/2025, ISA none at all), so 'the law as at 26 August 2026' is not a single vintage across the corpus. The line states when the consolidated text was last rebuilt; it does not certify that nothing has since been enacted. ISA1967 carries no such line, which I initially could not distinguish from a fetch/extraction defect and had to confirm separately against SSO.

searches.question: Has SSO's text changed since the 25–26 Aug 2026 fetch?
searches.scope: sso.agc.gov.sg Act pages for GIA1934, WA1838, ISA1967, PAA1934, AMLA1966
searches.query: curl -A <browser UA> https://sso.agc.gov.sg/Act/{GIA1934,WA1838,ISA1967,PAA1934,AMLA1966}; compare byte size to fetched .html
searches.coverage_note: All five returned byte-identical sizes to the fetched copies and all report 'Current version as at 26 Aug 2026'. Byte-size equality is a weak identity test — I compared sizes, not hashes, so a same-length substitution would pass. WebFetch returns HTTP 403 on SSO; only curl with a browser User-Agent works, so any future agent repeating this must not conclude from a WebFetch 403 that the page is gone.

searches.question: Which Acts are 'Act 25 of 2021', 'Act 3 of 2022', 'Act 18 of 2023', 'Act 24 of 2022'?
searches.scope: Open web plus SSO Acts Supplement browse for 2022 and 2023
searches.query: Singapore "Act 25 of 2021" AND "Act 3 of 2022" short titles legislation; SSO /Browse/Acts-Supp/Published/{2022,2023}
searches.coverage_note: Resolved to Courts (Civil and Criminal Justice) Reform Act 2021; Women's Charter (Amendment) Act 2022; Family Justice Reform Act 2023; Singapore Armed Forces and Other Matters Act 2022. The first two short titles came from an LLM summary of search results rather than a fetched gazette page; I corroborated Act 24 of 2022 and Act 18 of 2023 against the SSO Acts Supplement index directly, but did NOT separately open the gazette for Acts 25/2021 and 3/2022 to confirm their short titles, relying instead on their full text which I did fetch and read.

searches.question: Do the FJRA 2023, CCCJRA 2021 and WC(A)A 2022 contain provisions touching the four Acts that have NOT commenced?
searches.scope: Full gazette text of Act 18/2023, Act 25/2021, Act 3/2022
searches.query: curl SSO Acts-Supp PDFs; pdftotext; grep -niE 'Guardianship of Infants|Probate and Administration|Intestate Succession|Wills Act'; read s 1 commencement clause
searches.coverage_note: Found the complete set touching our Acts: FJRA ss 13, 14, 36; CCCJRA s 132; WC(A)A s 43(3). Every one is reflected in the fetched text with a wef date, so none is uncommenced. This checks only these three Acts — it is not a general statement that they are fully in force (FJRA s 1 splits commencement across four different Ministers and many sections unrelated to our corpus may still be pending; I did not enumerate those).

searches.question: Does the FJRA 2023 carry savings or transitional provisions that bound the temporal reach of the amended GIA and PAA text?
searches.scope: Act 18 of 2023 s 45
searches.query: sed -n '2890,2945p' of pdftotext output of Act 18/2023
searches.coverage_note: Found s 45(7), (10) and (11) bearing on GIA s 11 and PAA ss 4 and 39. I read s 45 subsections (4)–(12) only; I did NOT read s 45(1)–(3) or beyond (12), so further savings bearing on our Acts could exist in the parts of that long section I skipped. Savings in the OTHER two amending Acts (CCCJRA 2021, WC(A)A 2022) were not searched for at all.

searches.question: Did any bill from 2020–2026 amend any of the four Acts?
searches.scope: Every bill in the SSO Bills Supplement for 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 — 256 bills, downloaded as PDF and converted to text
searches.query: curl /Browse/Bills-Supp/Published/<year>?PageSize=100; download each Bills-Supp PDF; pdftotext -layout; grep -lE 'Guardianship of Infants|Probate and Administration Act|Intestate Succession Act|Wills Act'
searches.coverage_note: This is the search that found Finding 1, and the only method used here that can see an enacted-but-uncommenced amendment. Hits: 15/2022 (WA, Act 24/2022), 15/2023 (GIA, FJRA), 21/2023 (PAA, Act 25/2023 — THE finding), 36-2021, 43-2021, 18-2021, 6-2025. Limits, and they are real: (a) it greps BILLS as introduced, so an amendment inserted by committee amendment at second reading would be invisible; (b) it matches Act SHORT TITLES only — a bill amending our Acts via a Schedule that says merely 'section 7' under a heading, or via a generic formula like 'every written law', would be missed; (c) it stops at 2020, so a pre-2020 uncommenced amendment is out of scope; (d) I verified text extraction was non-empty for 2024–2026 but did NOT run that emptiness check for 2020–2023, so a silently-failed pdftotext in those years would read as a clean negative.

searches.question: Is there a 'Wills Bill' before Parliament proposing electronic execution and virtual witnessing?
searches.scope: Open web, then Parliament's bills-introduced index and the SSO Bills Supplement
searches.query: Singapore Bill 2026 wills probate succession estate amendment Parliament; "Wills Bill" Singapore Parliament 2025 introduced first reading
searches.coverage_note: REFUTED, and worth recording as a trap. An initial web search returned an LLM summary asserting a 'Wills Bill' was 'tabled in Parliament during the 2025 legislative session', 'subject of public consultation and select-committee review', and Singapore's 'most significant reform to will-execution rules in decades'. The sole basis was SEO marketing pages (globaladvisoryexperts.com, singaporefinance.sg, tembusulaw.com, litigaforge.com) that carry '2026' in their titles for freshness, not because they report 2026 events. No such bill exists: Parliament's own index (772 bills) returns nothing for 'wills', and the SSO Bills Supplement for 2025 (22 bills) and 2026 (18 bills) contains no Wills Bill. Do not re-import this claim.

searches.question: Does the Electronic Conveyancing and Other Matters Bill (2025) touch wills or succession?
searches.scope: MinLaw second reading speech, 15 October 2025
searches.query: WebFetch mlaw.gov.sg second-reading-speech-for-electronic-conveyancing-and-other-matters-bill
searches.coverage_note: It amends the Mental Capacity Act 2008 (remote witnessing of LPAs) and conveyancing law, not the Wills Act, PAA, ISA or GIA. Read via a summarising fetch of a MINISTERIAL SPEECH, not the bill text — a speech can omit a minor consequential amendment buried in a schedule. The bill itself is 12/2025 and WAS covered by the full-text 2025 bill grep above, which returned no hit, so the negative rests on that stronger check rather than on the speech.

searches.question: Does the Statutes (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill 12/2026 sweep in any of the four Acts?
searches.scope: Bill 12/2026 full text
searches.query: pdftotext of parliament.gov.sg bill PDF; grep for the four Act names and for 'Amendment of ... Act'
searches.coverage_note: Amends only MND-administered Acts: BCA Act 1999, Architects Act 1991, Professional Engineers Act 1991, Building (Strata Management) Act 2004, Housing and Development Act 1959, URA Act 1989, Wildlife Act 1965. Checked because these catch-all Acts are the classic vector for a quiet amendment. Covers this one bill only; the 2025 Statutes (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill was covered by the year-wide grep, not read individually.

searches.question: Has Act 25 of 2023 s 17 (inserting PAA s 28(3)) been brought into force?
searches.scope: Act 25 of 2023 s 1; Commencement Notification S 743/2023; SSO PAA1934 in-force text and amending-Act list
searches.query: curl https://sso.agc.gov.sg/SL-Supp/S743-2023/Published/20231116?DocDate=20231116&ViewType=Pdf; pdftotext
searches.coverage_note: S 743/2023 commences ss 5, 11, 12, 13, 15, 18, 19 and 20 on 1 Dec 2023 — s 17 is absent. Corroborated three ways: fetched PAA s 28 has only subsections (1) and (2); SSO's PAA amending-Act list omits Act 25 of 2023; a targeted web search for a No. 2 notification found none. THE WEAK LINK: I could not enumerate subsidiary legislation under Act 25 of 2023 directly — the SSO Act page is JS-rendered and returned only a 24KB shell to curl, and lawplain's subsidiary_legislation corpus returned zero results for this Act. So the absence of a LATER commencement notification rests on a negative web search plus the state of the in-force text, not on a definitive index read. searches.question: Has the age of majority, or the meaning of 'infant' in the GIA, changed?
searches.scope: Open web; GIA s 2; Civil Law Act 1909 s 35; Interpretation Act 1965
searches.query: Singapore age of majority 21 to 18 change 2025 2026 Civil Law Act section 35 review; grep source texts for 'majority', 'minor', 'infant'
searches.coverage_note: No change found. GIA s 2 defines only 'court' and never defines 'infant'; CLA s 35 lowers CONTRACTUAL capacity to 18 and s 35(3)(b) expressly preserves age thresholds in other written laws, so it does not reach the GIA. The only substantive material surfaced dates from the 2008–2009 reform. This is a search for a CHANGE, and it does not establish what the age actually is — the common-law majority of 21 is an inference from the absence of a statutory definition, not something I verified against authority. IA1965 has recent amendments (Act 19 of 2025 wef 5/12/2025) which I did not read; I only grepped it for 'majority'/'minor' and found nothing relevant.

searches.question: Has the Intestate Succession Act 1967 been amended at all since the 2020 Revised Edition?

searches.query: grep for bracketed amendment markers (zero found); SSO ISA1967 page parsed for 'Act N of 20NN' entries (zero found)
searches.coverage_note: Decisive negative, and the cleanest result in the sweep: ISA1967 carries no amendment markers, no 'Informal Consolidation' line, and SSO lists no amending Act. Reinforced by the 256-bill sweep, in which the only ISA hits were references, not amendments. Caveat: this speaks to the STATUTE only. ISA s 7 distribution rules are heavily litigated and case law can reinterpret them without a word of the text changing; judicial development is out of scope for this P2 lens and was not searched.

searches.question: Has the AMLA boundary that ISA s 2 routes Muslim estates into moved?

searches.coverage_note: ISA s 2 is self-contained ('Nothing in this Act shall apply to the estate of any Muslim'), so it does not move when AMLA moves. AMLA has in fact been amended heavily (Act 4 of 2024 with commencements to 7/8/2025, Act 5 of 2025) and Bill 3/2024 showed no inheritance/faraid hits. But I checked AMLA's INHERITANCE provisions only by keyword; I did not diff AMLA s 111–116 across versions, so a change to the Syariah Court's inheritance jurisdiction could have been missed. Surfaced separately that Act 25 of 2023 s 10 would delete AMLA s 109B and is likewise uncommenced (Finding 2).

searches.scope: lawplain judgments corpus (SGCA/SGHC/SGHCF/SGFC), all years

A targeted query for a case that actually decides the point ('"infant" defined under 21 years Guardianship of Infants Act jurisdiction ceases child attains 21') returned ZERO results. entries.summary: Family Justice (Probate and Other Matters) Rules 2024 P.6 r 24 is the strongest written-law anchor for 21 anywhere in the four-Act estate: a grant during infancy runs "until he or she attains 21 years of age". The PAA fixes no age — neither s 21 nor the s 2 interpretation section defines "infant" or names a number — and r 24 also supplies a ranked list of grantees (both parents jointly / statutory guardian / testamentary guardian / court-appointed guardian, with a Registrar-assigned override under r 24(3)) and a 16-year threshold at which the infant may nominate a next-of-kin, none of which is in the Act. r 24(6) makes the right unrenounceable on the infant's behalf; r 24(5) engages PAA s 6(2) where a minority forces two administrators. Caveat carried from the corroboration: 21 is probably declaratory of what "infant" already means, so the Rules are the only positive-law text stating the number, not necessarily its source.

entries.disposition_note: DEFERRED, and this is the register's centre of gravity. The Guardianship of Infants Act defines only "court" (s 2) and never defines "infant"; the Interpretation Act 1965 supplies no general age of majority and Civil Law Act 1909 s 35 is confined to contractual capacity, with s 35(3)(b) expressly preserving age requirements stated in other written laws — so nothing in the fetched sources fixes the age. What would have to be true for this to become `encoded`: the encoding carries the age as a named parameter with 21 as its value and cites this rule as the authority, rather than writing 21 as a constant. Writing 21 as a bare constant would be the right number reached by a route CLA s 35(3)(b) forecloses. Disposition written before the encoding was readable.

entries.summary: The only judicial statement surfaced on what "infant" means in the GIA is obiter: a parenthesis in the closing observation of a forum non conveniens judgment, which says an infant is "a child, who is less than 21 years old" and elsewhere calls 21 "the age of majority in Singapore" — citing no statute for either. The proposition is nevertheless operative: the court held it had no power to order maintenance under s 5 for a child who had turned 21, and contrasted Women's Charter s 69, which does permit maintenance beyond 21. The judge is Foo Tuat Yien JC; the sweep's original attribution to Debbie Ong JC was wrong and is corrected here.

provenance.quote: 64 I conclude with an observation. Section 5 of the Guardianship of Infants Act provides only for the maintenance of an infant (ie, a child, who is less than 21 years old). Although the mother filed her application one month before R became 21 years old, he is now an adult. Section 5 of the Guardianship of Infants Act does not empower a court to make an order for maintenance of a child beyond the age of 21. This is in contrast to s 12A of the HK Guardianship of Minors Ordinance and s 69 of the Women’s Charter, both of which allow a court to make orders for maintenance of a child beyond the age of 18 years (Hong Kong) and 21 years (Singapore). 65 Simply put, the court is no longer empowered to order maintenance in favour of R under s 5 of the Guardianship of Infants Act since he is now above the age of 21.

entries.summary: GIA s 11 (Matters to be considered) was wholly replaced with effect from 31 January 2024. The pre-amendment section required the court to consider only the wishes of the parent or parents; the replacement adds a second mandatory consideration in paragraph (b) — where the infant is of an age to express an independent opinion, the wishes of the infant — and changes "shall" to "must". Paragraph (b) adopts a formula long-standing in Women's Charter s 125(2)(b), so it aligns the GIA rather than creating a novel test. The gate has no statutory age attached and cannot be encoded as a numeric threshold.

The words "divorce" and "annulment" appear nowhere in the Act.

entries.summary: Wills Act s 6(2) permits a will to be SIGNED by another person in the testator's presence and by the testator's direction; it governs the signature only. In the most recent decision found on any of the four Acts, the court reasoned a fortiori from s 6(2) within the substantive-validity analysis: because the statute tolerates even the signature being made by another on the testator's direction, the fact that portions of the will were filled in by a third party on the testator's instructions was not, on those facts, a reason to suspect the execution. The corroboration corrects the pincite — s 6(2) is discussed only at [24]; [19]-[20] frame validity generally and cite s 6, not s 6(2).

provenance.source: General Division of the High Court, Mohamed Faizal J, 14 May 2026
provenance.citation: Fauziyah bte Mohd Ahbidin (executrix of the estate of Mohamed Ahbideen bin Mohamed Kassim (alias Ahna Mohamed Zainal Abidin bin Kassim), deceased) and another v Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura [2026] SGHC 104 at [24] (s 6(2) discussed only here; [19]-[20] frame validity generally and cite s 6, not s 6(2))
provenance.quote: Given that a testator’s will may be signed by someone other than the testator on the testator’s direction (see s 6(2) of the WA), the fact that certain portions of the Will were filled in on Kassim’s instructions is not a reason, on these facts at least, to cast suspicion on the execution of the Will. On the contrary, it supports its legitimacy as it hints to the fact that Kassim was made aware of, and assented to, the contents of the Will.

entries.disposition_note: NO EFFECT: nothing in the decision alters s 6(2), which is textually unamended since the 2020 Rev Ed consolidation in force from 28/10/2022. What the case does supply is the two-axis structure an encoding must keep separate — formal validity under s 6, and substantive validity (capacity, knowledge and approval, absence of undue influence) which lives entirely outside the Act. Encoding s 6 alone models only half of what makes a will good, and the judgment says so. Weight caveat: by closing submissions the defendant no longer contested validity, and the judge considered it "for good order".

entries.summary: The Wills Act applies to Muslims in full EXCEPT s 3, by AMLA 1966 s 111(2)(a) — so a Muslim's will must satisfy the s 6 formalities even though the power to dispose by will is governed by the school of Muslim law professed (AMLA s 111(1)). WA1838 contains no reference to Muslims anywhere, so an encoder working from the four Acts alone would either apply the whole Wills Act to Muslims or, reasoning by analogy from ISA s 2, exclude them entirely; both are wrong. AMLA s 111(2)(c) does the same for the whole Probate and Administration Act 1934, which therefore applies to Muslims unmodified. The corroboration corrects the citation: [2026] SGHC 104 does not cite Shafeeg and is an independent restatement, not an application of it.

provenance.source: Court of Appeal (2010); independently restated by the General Division of the High Court (2026)
provenance.citation: Shafeeg bin Salim Talib and another v Fatimah bte Abud bin Talib and others [2010] SGCA 11 at [71] (CA; Chan Sek Keong CJ, Andrew Phang Boon Leong JA, V K Rajah JA; 18 March 2010); the same construction of AMLA s 111(2)(a) was reached independently, WITHOUT citing Shafeeg, in Fauziyah bte Mohd Ahbidin (executrix of the estate of Mohamed Ahbideen bin Mohamed Kassim (alias Ahna Mohamed Zainal Abidin bin Kassim), deceased) and another v Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura [2026] SGHC 104 at [20] (General Division; Mohamed Faizal J; 14 May 2026) — https://www.elitigation.sg/gd/s/2026_SGHC_104
provenance.quote: Finally, s 111(2)(a) of the AMLA provides that nothing in that section shall affect the provisions of the Wills Act, other than s 3 thereof. A will executed by a Muslim therefore has to comply with the formalities prescribed by s 6 of the Wills Act which requires a will to be in writing and executed in accordance with s 6(2). Expanding the applicability of s 111(1) of the AMLA to the right of survivorship would negate the formal requirements of a will. We reject this argument.

entries.disposition_note: SCOPED OUT: ISA s 2 routes Muslim estates out of this corpus, and AMLA1966 is carried in the bundle as corroboration for that boundary rather than as a modelled source. The cost is precise and worth stating: the scope-out is correct for intestacy and wrong for wills, because the carve-out is surgical — s 3 out, everything else including s 6 in — so an encoding that extends to Muslim wills must NOT reuse the ISA s 2 exclusion. Recorded here so that trap is on the record even though this corpus does not walk into it.

entries.summary: No Singapore court has read down Wills Act s 13, and this is a negative dressed as a finding: three differently-phrased searches produced no case construing s 13 itself, only cases where its automatic operation was the motive for attacking the triggering marriage. Tan Ah Thee is good authority that Women's Charter s 105 states its grounds of voidness exhaustively. But the corroboration establishes that the further claim — that the courts have refused to disapply s 13 by declaring the marriage void — is NO LONGER accurate: Gian Bee Choo [2019] SGHC 179 and Kee Cheong Keng [2025] SGHCF 15 both declared pre-1-October-2016 marriages of convenience void, and Soon Ah See [2016] SGHC 185 at [52] read down the direct analogue in CPF Act s 25(5)(a), reasoning expressly from Wills Act s 13(1).

provenance.source: High Court (2009), with the later line traced by the corroboration
provenance.citation: Tan Ah Thee and another (administrators of the estate of Tan Kiam Poh (alias Tan Gna Chua), deceased) v Lim Soo Foong [2009] SGHC 101 at [40], [53]-[56] (primary; s 105 exhaustive, attack on will-revoking marriage rejected); Toh Seok Kheng v Huang Huiqun [2010] SGHC 308 at [12], [17] (s 105 exhaustiveness only - an intestacy case, no will and no s 13 issue); Soon Ah See and another v Diao Yanmei [2016] SGHC 185 at [52]-[53] (read down the analogous CPF Act s 25(5)(a) automatic revocation, reasoning expressly from Wills Act s 13(1)); contra Gian Bee Choo and others v Meng Xianhui [2019] SGHC 179 at [95]-[96], [101] and Kee Cheong Keng v Dinh Thi Thu Hien [2025] SGHCF 15 at [9]-[11] (pre-2016 marriage of convenience declared void); Cheng Tze Tzuen v Dang Lan Anh [2025] SGHC 112 at [16], [29]-[33] (reaffirming Tan Ah Thee, disagreeing with Gian Bee Choo; on appeal to the Appellate Division per [10])
provenance.quote: In short, the plaintiffs’ argument was, once again, that the court can declare a marriage void on a ground other than those provided for in s 105 of the Charter. As explained above, with regard to the lack of valid consent, this proposition contradicts s 105 which states the grounds listed therein to be exclusive. Hence, this argument must fail for this reason alone.

entries.disposition_note: SCOPED OUT: whether a marriage is void is decided under the Women's Charter, which this corpus does not model — see E20, where the same split does its damage on the ISA side. s 13(1) can be encoded as written (marriage revokes the will, automatically, no judicial discretion to relieve), but the encoding must not treat "was married" as settled for a pre-1-October-2016 marriage. Two blind spots carried forward rather than closed: nothing whatever was found on s 13(2), the "expressed to be made in contemplation of a marriage" exception including its polygamy clause, which remains entirely unswept (S6); and the Soon Ah See reasoning transfers to s 13 on its face and has never been tested there.

entries.summary: The Court of Appeal proceeded on the footing that ISA s 3 defines "child" as a legitimate child (plus a child adopted by order of court), so an illegitimate child does not take the child's share under s 7 Rule 3. The statements are reasoning supporting a holding on a different Act — the Inheritance (Family Provision) Act — not a decision on the ISA. The corroboration is emphatic that the exclusion is NOT absolute, and the same judgment says so at [18] and [20]: Legitimacy Act 1934 s 10(1) admits an illegitimate child to the MOTHER's intestacy where she leaves no legitimate issue, and LA ss 3 and 5 admit a person legitimated by the parents' subsequent marriage.

provenance.source: Court of Appeal
provenance.citation: AAG v Estate of AAH, deceased [2009] SGCA 56 at [22], [38(c)] (Court of Appeal, 19 November 2009); cf [18] and [20] on Legitimacy Act 1934 s 10(1)
provenance.quote: At this juncture, it may be pertinent to refer to the Intestate Succession Act (Cap 146, 1985 Rev Ed) where s 3 provides that a "child" means a "legitimate child". Thus, the Intestate Succession Act excludes an illegitimate child from succeeding to his or her parent's intestate estate, unlike his or her legitimate siblings.

entries.disposition_note: NO EFFECT: the construction confirms the literal reading of s 3, so nothing has to be re-encoded — but it forecloses the purposive escape route an encoder might assume exists, and the CA reinforced the exclusion by refusing to let the IFPA be used to circumvent it. The qualification that DOES change the answer is not in this entry: it is E17, the Legitimacy Act. ISA s 3 must not be encoded as "illegitimate implies takes nothing on intestacy". The CA urged legislative reform at [41]-[43]; ten years on nothing has been enacted (E24, E26).

entries.summary: A foster child falls outside the ambit of the ISA: s 3's "means ... and includes" admits a legitimate child and, only to that extent, a child adopted by order of court. The claimant produced two inconsistently translated PRC notarial certificates, an ancestral book, funeral photographs and a tombstone bearing his name; none proved adoption. Two limits the corroboration insists on: the court REJECTED the evidence of the relationship, so this is not authority that a proven, long-standing foster relationship is nonetheless excluded; and although the court recited s 3's confinement to orders of court under written law in force in Singapore, Malaysia or Brunei Darussalam, it did not decide whether a foreign adoption order qualifies.

provenance.source: High Court
provenance.citation: Lim Weipin and another v Lim Boh Chuan and others [2010] SGHC 99, [2010] 3 SLR 423 (Tan Lee Meng J, 30 March 2010) at [33], [56] and [60]; for the exclusivity of the s 3 definition see Low Guang Hong David and others v Suryono Wino Goei [2012] SGHC 93 at [15], [18] and [20]
provenance.quote: There is a yet another reason why LW did not establish that he is LHC's adopted son. While an adopted child is entitled under the Act to a share of the deceased's parent's estate, a foster child is outside the ambit of the Act. ... I thus find that LW did not prove that he was an adopted son rather than a foster son. As such, he has no claim to LHC's assets under the Act. ["There is a yet another reason" is sic in the original; the ellipsis spans [57]-[59]. Verified character-for-character against the lawplain full text of 2010_SGHC_99.]

entries.disposition_note: NO EFFECT: confirms that adoptive status is a formal, evidenced predicate rather than a functional one, which is how a definition-driven encoding would already treat it. What it does NOT settle is the question an encoder most needs answered — whether a foreign adoption order can ever satisfy s 3. That point is textual and untested, and the encoding should expose it rather than resolve it. S2's own coverage note is candid that six hits for a question this central is thin, and that the complementary searches (Adoption of Children Act 2022, legitimation under the Legitimacy Act, foreign adoption orders) were never run.

entries.summary: The Legitimacy Act 1934 rewrites who counts as entitled on an ISA intestacy, and the ISA never mentions it. s 10(1) admits an illegitimate child — or, if that child is dead, the child's issue — to the MOTHER's intestacy, on two conditions: the child is not a legitimated person, and the mother leaves no legitimate ISSUE surviving ("issue", not merely "child", so a predeceased legitimate child's descendants still bar the claim). s 10(2) runs the other way, giving the mother the parental share on the child's intestacy. ss 5, 6, 7 and 9 admit legitimated persons, and persons recognised as legitimated under foreign law, as if born legitimate — so legitimacy is a status that can be acquired after birth and dated, and the ISA test is legitimacy at the intestate's DEATH, not at the child's birth. This entry also carries the sweep's separate finding that the Court of Appeal noted s 10(1) in AAG v Estate of AAH at [18] and [20]; the load-bearing authority is the statute, in force since 18 May 1934, not the case.

provenance.source: Singapore Statutes Online, current version as at 26 Aug 2026, fetched live; judicially noted by the Court of Appeal
provenance.citation: Legitimacy Act 1934, ss 5, 6, 7, 9 and 10 (2020 Rev Ed; informal consolidation, version in force from 5 Dec 2025)
provenance.quote: 10.—(1) Where, on or after 18 May 1934, the mother of an illegitimate child, the child not being a legitimated person, dies intestate as respects all or any of her property, and does not leave any legitimate issue her surviving, the illegitimate child, or if he is dead his issue, shall be entitled to take any interest therein to which he or his issue would have been entitled if he had been born legitimate. (2) Where, on or after 18 May 1934, an illegitimate child, not being a legitimated person, dies intestate as respects all or any of his property, his mother, if surviving, shall be entitled to take any interest therein to which she would have been entitled if the child had been born legitimate and she had been the only surviving parent.

entries.disposition_note: DEFERRED, and it is the largest correctness gap in the register. What would have to be true for this to become `encoded`: the Legitimacy Act 1934 is fetched into the source bundle and its ss 5-7, 9 and 10 encoded alongside ISA ss 3 and 7. It is NOT among the fetched sources. Until it is, an encoding driven only by ISA ss 3 and 7 produces the wrong distribution for a mother's estate leaving illegitimate but no legitimate issue — an asymmetry invisible from the ISA text, where the exclusion is absolute for a male intestate and conditional for a female one. Note the interaction with Rule 3: s 10(1) fires only when the legitimate-issue set is empty. The Act's only recent change is terminological (E46).

entries.summary: ISA s 7 Rule 9 was construed — obiter — as applying only where Rules 1 to 8 fail WHOLLY, not where they fail in part, for instance where one beneficiary (here a deported and untraceable surviving spouse) cannot be found. Read consistently with Civil Law Act 1909 s 27(1)(a), which speaks of persons "who have died intestate without next-of-kin". This is the most encoding-relevant construction in the sweep: Rule 9's trigger, "in default of distribution under rules 1 to 8", is exactly the catch-all a formaliser encodes as a fallback branch that fires whenever the preceding rules do not fully distribute — and read that way it would hand the State an untraceable spouse's half share. WEIGHT: not a holding. The court made no order, framed the passage as what the claimant may argue before the Family Justice Courts, said the matter "was not properly before me", and hedged the reasoning as "implying that".

provenance.source: General Division of the High Court, Valerie Thean J
provenance.citation: Cheng Tze Tzuen v Dang Lan Anh [2025] SGHC 112 at [47] (obiter), General Division of the High Court, Valerie Thean J, 1 July 2025 (HC/OA 1057/2024)
provenance.quote: While Rule 9 is stated to apply "in default of distribution under Rules 1 to 8", this serves to entitle the Government to the whole of the estate, implying that Rule 9 applies only where Rules 1 to 8 has wholly, and not partially, failed. Such a reading is consistent with s 27(1)(a) of the Civil Law Act 1909 (2020 Rev Ed) which refers to the right accruing to Government where persons "who have died intestate without next-of-kin" (emphasis added).

entries.disposition_note: SUBSUMED into the partial-failure case, which this corpus does not model: the construction only bites where Rules 1 to 8 partially fail, and the remedy the same judgment identifies for that case — a Benjamin order redistributing on assumed facts without extinguishing the absent beneficiary's entitlement — is procedural relief outside these four Acts. Read the note rather than the enum: this construction is NOT known to be reflected in the encoding, and it must be. It would be disposed `deferred` but for the schema rule that an interpretive entry disposed `deferred` must name a fork, and this encoding has no fork register yet (see the register note). The paragraph also records a genuine statutory gap — where the administrator cannot establish whether the spouse is alive, "The Rules do not stipulate". Currency risk: the decision is under appeal, though on a different point (E20).

entries.summary: PAA s 18(4)(a) lists "the husband or widow or next of kin or any of them" as an unordered set and s 18(4)(b) makes the choice among them discretionary; the courts supply the missing order and import it wholesale from a different Act. Priority to a grant follows priority of beneficial entitlement to the estate under ISA s 7, because the beneficiary with the greatest entitlement is the person most interested in it. Two rungs are established by authority — spouse ahead of PARENT (Toh Seok Kheng, the ratio on those facts) and spouse ahead of CHILD (Cheng Tze Tzuen at [39]). Child ahead of parent is NOT adjudicated; it follows from ISA s 7 itself (r 3 gives the estate to issue subject to the spouse; r 5 admits parents only if there are no descendants).

provenance.source: High Court (2010), applied by the General Division of the High Court (2025)
provenance.citation: Toh Seok Kheng v Huang Huiqun [2010] SGHC 308, [2011] 1 SLR 737, at [23]-[24] (High Court, Judith Prakash J) - spouse ahead of parent; applied in Cheng Tze Tzuen v Dang Lan Anh [2025] SGHC 112 at [39] (General Division of the High Court, Valerie Thean J) - spouse ahead of child. Further corroborated by Chye Hwa Luan and others v Do, Allyn T [2023] SGHCR 10 at [35(a)] (ss 18(2) and (4) are the priority provisions); Family Justice (Probate and Other Matters) Rules 2024 (S 723/2024) P. 6 r. 16(1); and G Raman, Probate and Administration in Singapore and Malaysia (LexisNexis, 4th Ed, 2018) at paras 7.31-7.32 (cited in Cheng Tze Tzuen at [39]; not independently verified). Caveat: Cheng Tze Tzuen is under appeal (at [10]), but on its void-marriage holding, not on [39]; no appellate decision found as at 2026-08-26. Text of s 18(2) and (4)(a)-(b) verified identical between the Cap 251, 2000 Rev Ed construed in 2010 and the 2020 Rev Ed in force from 15/10/2024, so no amendment has mooted the construction.
provenance.quote: Although where a person dies intestate, the court has a discretion under s 18, PAA as to whom to appoint as the administrator of the deceased’s estate, the starting point is that the person who is most suitable among the beneficiaries to be the administrator is determined according to the priorities of entitlement to the deceased’s estate under the laws of intestate succession. This is because the beneficiary with the greatest entitlement to the deceased’s estate will naturally be the person most interested in the estate of the deceased. [23] ... The defendant, being the deceased’s surviving spouse, had priority of entitlement to the estate by virtue of s 7 of the ISA and she had a corresponding prior right over the plaintiff, who was the deceased’s parent, in obtaining a grant of letters of administration of the estate. [24]

entries.disposition_note: SUBSUMED into the ISA s 7 distribution order this corpus already has to encode: s 18(4)(b) contributes no independent ranking, so encoding the two Acts against one ontology is what makes the construction operative. The previous three-Act register disposed the same holding as `encoded` against a fork; the fork register for this encoding does not exist yet, so that link cannot be re-made here and this entry does not claim it. Two consequences to carry: every contested question about ISA s 7's "surviving spouse" (E20, E21, E22) propagates directly into who may take the grant; and the ordering assumes ISA distribution, so it does not govern Muslim estates, for which PAA s 18(5) preserves special provision. Text of s 18(2) and (4) verified identical between the 2000 and 2020 Rev Eds, so no amendment has mooted it.

entries.summary: The ISA does not define "spouse" — s 3 defines only "child", "intestate" and "issue" — so the "surviving spouse" predicate in s 7 Rules 1 to 8, and through it priority under PAA s 18, depends on an antecedent question of marriage validity decided under the Women's Charter. On that question two General Division judges split in 2025 over whether a marriage of convenience solemnised BEFORE 1 October 2016 can be declared void, WC ss 11A and 105(aa) being expressly confined to marriages on or after that date. Kee Cheong Keng, following Gian Bee Choo, declared a 2013 marriage void; Cheng Tze Tzuen respectfully disagreed, holding that this writes words into the statute. Neither court decided the ISA s 7 or PAA s 18 question. This entry also carries the sweep's separate finding on the PENDING APPEAL: the claimant in Cheng Tze Tzuen has appealed to the Appellate Division, and the corroboration is firm that the register must NOT say the appeal "will resolve" the conflict — the judge made no order on the ground that the relief was misconceived and the proper forum was the Family Justice Courts, so the appeal may be disposed of on that footing without reaching s 11A.

provenance.source: General Division of the High Court (Family Division), Choo Han Teck J, 28 Feb 2025; and General Division of the High Court, Valerie Thean J, 1 Jul 2025
provenance.citation: Kee Cheong Keng v Dinh Thi Thu Hien [2025] SGHCF 15 (Choo Han Teck J, HCF/Suit No 4 of 2022, decided 28 Feb 2025) at [7], [9]-[10]; contra Cheng Tze Tzuen v Dang Lan Anh [2025] SGHC 112 (Valerie Thean J, HC/OA 1057/2024, decided 1 Jul 2025) at [13]-[14], [22], [29]-[33], [35], [39], [45(b)], [46]-[47], [50]. Earlier limb of the split: Gian Bee Choo and others v Meng Xianhui [2019] 5 SLR 812 at [89], [101], [130]-[131], [137], [139], [146]. Contrary line preferred by Thean J: Tan Ah Thee v Lim Soo Foong [2009] 3 SLR(R) 957 at [54]-[57]; Toh Seok Kheng v Huang Huiqun [2011] 1 SLR 737 at [12]-[15], [23]-[24]; Soon Ah See v Diao Yanmei [2016] 5 SLR 693 at [35], [39]-[45], [48]. Statutory frame: Women's Charter 1961 ss 11A, 13(a), 16(2)(a), 17(1)(b), 104, 105(a) and 105(aa) (s 11A and s 105(aa) confined to marriages solemnised on or after 1 October 2016, unamended as at 26 Aug 2026); ISA 1967 ss 3 and 7 Rules 1-9; PAA 1934 s 18. STATUS: appeal against [2025] SGHC 112 recorded as filed at [10]; no appellate decision located as at 26 Aug 2026, and the searches run reach reliably only to about mid-May 2026 (see search record). Consequential application to Wills Act 1838 s 13 is inference, not holding; nearest judicial anchor is In the Estate of Park, decd [1954] P 112, cited at [45(b)].
provenance.quote: Kee Cheong Keng at [10]: "Public policy requires this court to declare the sham marriage void and not permit the “spouse” of a sham marriage to inherit the other party's assets." || Cheng Tze Tzuen at [30]: "I respectfully disagree that a marriage certificate would be invalidated by a failure to declare an intention to enter a marriage of convenience. In my respectful view, this approach would amount to stipulating a new ground under s 105 of the WC or extending the applicable time period specified in ss 11A and 105(aa) of the WC. It is, in essence, writing words into the statute." || Kee Cheong Keng at [7], on the limit of what was decided: "This was a civil suit, and the jurisdiction of the court was limited to the determination of the validity of the marriage." || Cheng Tze Tzuen at [39], making the PAA s 18 / ISA s 7 link explicit: "the Defendant (as the spouse) would have priority to the letters of administration vis-à-vis the Claimant (as the child), the entitlement to which is prescribed by s 18 of the Probate and Administration Act 1934 (2020 Rev Ed) (“PAA”). Entitlement to the letters of administration is based on priority of entitlement to the estate under s 7 of the Intestate Succession Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed) (“ISA”)". || Cheng Tze Tzuen at [46], leaving the door open: "There could be a basis for taking public policy considerations into account in the exercise of that discretion, with application of the UKM two-stage analytical framework." [Composite of five passages from two judgments; each verbatim, joined here by ‖.]

entries.disposition_note: SCOPED OUT: marriage validity is decided under the Women's Charter, which is not in this bundle and which this corpus does not model. The cost is that "surviving spouse" — the top-level discriminator in ISA s 7, which selects between Rules 1, 2 and 4 and fixes the size of every other share — is being taken as given by an encoding that cannot compute it. It should be exposed as an open parameter for pre-1-October-2016 marriages, not silently resolved. Currency risk is real and unresolved: pendency as at 26 Aug 2026 is INFERRED from silence (S16 could not distinguish "not yet decided" from "decided but not yet ingested", and the appellate corpus edge is early June 2026), and the split runs back to 2019, not 2025. Direction of travel matters downstream: if the marriage is void ab initio then Wills Act s 13 never revoked any earlier will either (E14).

entries.summary: A spouse of a merely VOIDABLE marriage remains a "spouse" within ISA s 7: a judgment of nullity for a voidable marriage operates only from the time it is made final (WC s 110(2)), so the survivor was the deceased's wife immediately prior to death, and the marriage was in any event already dissolved by death. She also retains her prior right to letters of representation as widow, which feeds PAA s 18. The passage is obiter — counsel did not run the argument — and restates Tan Ah Thee, which is the primary authority.

provenance.source: High Court, Judith Prakash J (obiter, restating Tan Ah Thee)
provenance.citation: Toh Seok Kheng v Huang Huiqun [2010] SGHC 308, [2011] 1 SLR 737 at [20] (Judith Prakash J, High Court, 20 October 2010) (obiter, restating Tan Ah Thee and another (administrators of the estate of Tan Kiam Poh (alias Tan Gna Chua), deceased) v Lim Soo Foong [2009] SGHC 101, [2009] 3 SLR(R) 957 at [21], [26], [28], [30] and [31]); followed on ISA s 7 in Cheng Tze Tzuen v Dang Lan Anh [2025] SGHC 112 at [39]
provenance.quote: Thirdly, a judgment of nullity only operates from the time the judgment was made final. This meant that the defendant, as the deceased's wife immediately prior to his death, qualified as his "spouse" within the meaning of s 7 of the ISA. Hence, she would still be entitled to her share of the estate even if a declaration of nullity on the basis of a voidable marriage was obtained on the plaintiff's application, and she would also retain her prior right to apply for letters of representation as the deceased's widow. Finally, the marriage between the deceased and the defendant had already been dissolved by the death of the deceased under s 7(a) of the Charter. Since the marriage was no longer in existence, it could not be declared void for the future.

entries.disposition_note: SCOPED OUT for the same reason as E20: the void/voidable line is drawn under the Women's Charter. It is recorded because it draws that line exactly where an encoding needs it — voidness is retrospective and defeats spousal status, voidability is prospective and does not, so the predicate is "was lawfully married immediately prior to death", evaluated at the moment of death and undisturbed by a later nullity judgment on voidable grounds. It is also what makes E20 consequential: only if a marriage is void ab initio, not merely voidable, does spousal status disappear.

entries.summary: ISA s 8 presupposes that an intestate may leave "more than one wife" but says nothing about when that is possible; the answer is entirely external. Women's Charter s 4(1) makes a person lawfully married on 15 September 1961 incapable of contracting a further valid marriage, s 5(1) makes such a marriage void, and s 5(2) denies a woman who contracts a union with an already-married man any right of succession or inheritance on his intestacy — while s 181 preserves unions valid under custom before that date. The case is authority for the ESCAPE rather than the bar: the court declared the claimant a lawful wife of a pre-1961 Chinese customary secondary marriage and allowed her claim. The corroboration notes the judgment never cites ISA s 8, so the extension to s 8 is inference.

provenance.source: High Court, Woo Bih Li J
provenance.citation: Wong Swee Hor v Tan Jip Seng and others [2014] SGHC 263 (SGHC, Woo Bih Li J, 16 December 2014) at [25]–[28] (Women's Charter ss 181, 4(1), 5(1)–(2)), [76]–[77] (link to ISA s 7 r 2 "surviving spouse"), [218] and [234]–[236] (outcome)
provenance.quote: [28] "Mr Tan was already married to Mdm Owyang before the cut-off date of 15 September 1961. It was common ground that if he did marry Mdm Wong, this was after he had married Mdm Owyang. Therefore, Mdm Wong had to prove that she was lawfully married to Mr Tan under the law, religion, custom or usage prior to the cut-off date otherwise her marriage to Mr Tan would be void." … [218] "After considering all the evidence in totality, I found, on a balance of probabilities, that Mdm Wong is Mr Tan's lawful wife." … [235] "In conclusion, I allowed Mdm Wong's claim and declared that Mdm Wong is the lawful wife of Mr Tan."

entries.disposition_note: SCOPED OUT: the bar and its escape live in the Women's Charter, which this corpus does not model. What survives for the encoder is the shape of s 8's domain — a dated, closed and shrinking class, confined to unions valid under custom before 15 September 1961, and narrowed further because Muslims are already routed out by ISA s 2. s 8 should not be modelled as a general polygamy rule.

entries.summary: ISA s 2 reads as a clean total exclusion — "Nothing in this Act shall apply to the estate of any Muslim" — but the harder problem sits one level down, in what "estate" denotes, and the answer differs by personal law: for a deceased Muslim, what assets constitute the estate and effects under AMLA s 112(1) is determined first according to his personal law, not the common law, though only "where applicable to the circumstances" — where a general statute governs and contains no Muslim carve-out, the statute prevails. Applying that, survivorship under Land Titles Act s 114 extinguished the deceased's interest in jointly held registered land, so it never entered the distributable estate; the position for joint tenancy of PERSONAL property was expressly left open. The corroboration corrects the pincite: [76] is the costs paragraph.

provenance.source: Court of Appeal
provenance.citation: Shafeeg bin Salim Talib and another v Fatimah bte Abud bin Talib and others [2010] SGCA 11, [2010] 2 SLR 1123 (Court of Appeal; Chan Sek Keong CJ, Andrew Phang Boon Leong JA, V K Rajah JA; 18 March 2010) at [27] (what constitutes the estate) and [43]-[45] (survivorship extinguishes the interest), cf [28] and [44] (general statute prevails over personal law) and [46] (position for joint personal property left open). Affirming [2009] SGHC 100, [2009] 3 SLR(R) 439. Pin-cite [76] in the original register entry is wrong: [76] is the concluding disposition paragraph on costs.
provenance.quote: [27] We agree with the Judge's view that the meaning of the phrase "estate and effects" of the Deceased is a matter of statutory construction under the general law but, in our view, this does not mean that the court does not have to take into account Muslim law. ... The question as to what assets constitute the estate and effects of a deceased Muslim has first to be determined according to his personal law, where applicable to the circumstances, and not according to the common law. [45] For these reasons, we hold that the interest of the Deceased in the Property ceased to exist or was extinguished upon his death and, accordingly, his estate and effects distributable under s 112(1) of the AMLA in accordance with Muslim law did not include the Property or the Half Share upon the death of the Deceased.

entries.disposition_note: SCOPED OUT: ISA s 2 routes Muslim estates out of this corpus and AMLA1966 is carried only as corroboration for that boundary. One unresolved drafting gap is recorded rather than closed, because it is visible on the face of the two texts and no case resolving it was found: ISA s 2 excludes "any Muslim" with NO domicile qualifier, while AMLA s 112(1) applies only to a "Muslim person domiciled in Singapore" — leaving a non-domiciled Muslim outside both regimes on a literal reading. S4's own coverage note is blunt that the boundary is exactly where the corpora consulted are weakest: no Syariah Court judgments and no MUIS fatwas are in any corpus searched, and the Court of Appeal itself had to reason about fatwas 20 and 41 from secondary description.

entries.summary: The Government committed in March 2015 to review the Guardianship of Infants Act, the Intestate Succession Act, the Inheritance (Family Provision) Act and the Legitimacy Act, aiming to complete the work in 2016; the January 2016 Addendum to the President's Address restated it more narrowly, naming three Acts and no completion date. What landed from that programme was the maintenance-enforcement half — the Women's Charter (Amendment) Act 2022, the Family Justice Reform Act 2023, and the Maintenance Enforcement Process operationalised in January 2025. The substantive succession half did not: as at 26 August 2026 the ISA has never been amended, and no Intestate Succession (Amendment) Bill has ever been introduced.

Read correctly it is evidence of the ISA's stability rather than of impending reform — the register should say the announced reform is ten years old and undelivered, and an encoding stated as at 26 August 2026 can rely on that. The currency_risk flag is forced by the schema for an undated prospective item and should be read as "undated", not as "imminent".

entries.summary: At MinLaw's Committee of Supply on 2 March 2026 the Minister for Law named arbitration, corporate insolvency and IP as the year's legislative reviews. No amendment to the four Acts was announced or proposed. Two qualifications the corroboration insists on: the list is expressly non-exhaustive ("This will include") and the same debate adds a fourth Bill on civil judgment enforcement, so absence cannot be inferred from the quote alone; and wills WERE squarely on the agenda — an MP asked MinLaw to waive SAL Wills Registry fees and to regulate non-lawyer will-writers, and the Government declined both, proposing no change to the Wills Act.

The corroboration corrects the target: the sub-committee's named statutory object was the Inheritance (Family Provision) Act 1966, NOT ISA s 3. The work passed to MinLaw, which named the ISA in 2015 and 2016 (E24) and has not delivered; MSF said in November 2025 there are no current plans to review the term "illegitimacy".

entries.disposition_note: NO EFFECT, and it is the closest thing to formal reform pressure on the ISA's exclusion of illegitimate children — which is to say, very little. For the encoding: state the exclusion as the law and do not hedge it as under reform; it is stable, contested only in commentary, and has attracted no legislative or institutional action in fourteen years. Two limits on the negative. S51 could not reach a complete SAL index (older reports are bundled into year-grouped ZIPs that were not opened), so "no report published" is a reading of an incomplete index rather than a confirmed fact. And S58 reached no Singapore family-law scholarship at all — Leong Wai Kum and Debbie Ong are behind paywalls — so the field is represented here by a fourteen-year-old article by an Australian comparativist whose own assessment is that Singapore commentary is "scarce" and "descriptive".

entries.summary: THE HEADLINE CURRENCY RISK. Oaths, Declarations and Notarisations (Remote Methods) Act 2023 (Act 25 of 2023) s 17 would insert a new PAA s 28(3) deeming the requirement that a grantee appear before the person administering the administration oath to be satisfied where the oath is taken through electronic means prescribed in the Family Justice Rules. It was passed on 2 August 2023 and first published on 4 September 2023, and is STILL NOT IN FORCE as at 26 August 2026 — three years — with no commencement date appointed under s 1. Verified against two independent corpora: the fetched PAA and lawplain's current PAA both show s 28 with subsections (1) and (2) only, and no section of the PAA carries an [Act 25 of 2023 wef ...] annotation. Commencement notification S 743/2023 could not be retrieved directly; its effect is corroborated indirectly by SSO's per-provision annotations, and the sweep's original quotation of it has been withdrawn as unverified.

entries.summary: Two things an encoding of PAA s 18 needs and cannot get from the Act's own text. The forum moved: probate proceedings under the PAA are family proceedings within the Family Justice Courts' jurisdiction, by Family Justice Act 2014 s 2 read with s 22, so "the court" in the PAA means the FJC for these purposes by force of an external Act. And priority under s 18 is DEFEASIBLE through a specific procedural chain — a citation under s 4(1) issued under the Family Justice (Probate and Other Matters) Rules 2024 P 6 rr 38-39, deemed renunciation under s 4(2) on failure to file a notice of intention to contest, then preclusion under s 5(1) — which turns an apparently absolute ranking into a conditional one. Obiter guidance given while making no order.

provenance.source: General Division of the High Court, Valerie Thean J (obiter)
provenance.citation: Cheng Tze Tzuen v Dang Lan Anh [2025] SGHC 112 at [38]-[40]
provenance.quote: Under s 2 read with s 22 of the Family Justice Act 2014 (2020 Rev Ed), probate proceedings under the PAA constitute family proceedings and therefore fall under the jurisdiction of the FJC. In a case such as the present, the Claimant may cause a citation to be issued to the Defendant, pursuant to P 6 rr 38 and 39 of the Probate Rules: see s 4(1) of the PAA. The failure of the Defendant to file a notice of intention to contest or not contest in response to the citation would be deemed to be a renunciation of the prior right to letters of administration: s 4(2) of the PAA. This would have the effect of precluding any Defendant so renouncing from applying thereafter for the letters of administration: s 5(1) of the PAA. The Claimant, as the next person entitled to the letters of administration, would then be able to apply to the FJC for the letters of administration.

entries.disposition_note: SCOPED OUT: forum and procedure are not modelled by this corpus, which encodes entitlement rather than the route to a grant. The cost is that s 18 priority (E19) reads as absolute in the encoding when it is defeasible in practice. Provenance limit carried forward: the operative detail lives in the probate rules, and the pinpoints to P 6 rr 3, 38 and 39 are the judgment's, not verified at source — S7 did not fetch those rules, and S44 read Part 6 rules 1, 3, 23-28 and 31-33 but not rr 38-39.

entries.summary: Where there is a minority interest in the estate, a grantee of letters of administration from a Family Court must give security by way of an administration bond and 2 sureties. The trigger is BROADER than the Act's own, and the corroboration corrects the sweep on this point: PAA s 29(8) already requires security where "the person for whose use and benefit the grant is made is an infant" (s 29(8)(a)) or where the Family Court thinks fit (s 29(8)(b)), so this is not a gate the Act leaves entirely to the rules. What the Practice Direction does is convert s 29(8)(b)'s case-by-case discretion into six standing categories and extend the minority trigger to any "minority interest in the estate" — reaching estates granted to adult administrators who merely have a minor among the beneficiaries. Not an absolute bar: sureties may be dispensed with under s 29(3), and the Rules require 2 sureties only "except ... where the Registrar otherwise directs". The earlier "read with s 6(2)" pin is unsupported; the nearest real link is s 6(3).

provenance.source: Family Justice Courts electronic Practice Directions, live page confirmed 2026-08-26; Family Justice (Probate and Other Matters) Rules 2024
provenance.citation: Family Justice Courts Practice Directions 2024, para 214(2)(b) (minority trigger); Family Justice (Probate and Other Matters) Rules 2024 (S 723/2024), Part 6, r 31(2) (2-sureties default, subject to the Registrar directing otherwise); cf Probate and Administration Act 1934 ss 29(8), 29(3), 6(3), and PD para 215 (dispensation)
provenance.quote: (2) A grantee of letters of administration, whether with or without a will annexed, from a Family Court must give security for the due administration of the estate by way of an administration bond and 2 sureties in the following circumstances: (a) where the estate and effects in respect of which the grant is applied for, exclusive of what the deceased was possessed of or entitled to as a trustee and not beneficially, but without deducting anything on account of the debts due or owing from the deceased, exceed the value of $5 million; (b) where there is a minority interest in the estate; (c) where there is a life interest in the estate; (d) where there are beneficiaries who lack capacity within the meaning of the Mental Capacity Act 2008; (e) where the grantee is a creditor; and (f) in such other cases as the Registrar thinks fit.
