What would have to be true for this to become `encoded`: the PAA leg carries the asymmetry — a Family DIVISION grantee gives a bond and 2 sureties in every case, whereas a Family COURT grantee gives one only in the six listed circumstances, of which minority is one — and treats it as a gate on whether the grant issues rather than as advice. Class caveat kept deliberately: the Rules limb is subsidiary legislation and squarely binding, but the limb carrying the minority trigger is a Practice Direction issued by the Presiding Judge — mandatory in terms and gating registry practice, but neither a judgment nor an enactment. Currency risk because Practice Directions change without a gazette; E33 records that Part 24 was diffed and is unchanged today.

entries.summary: The probate rules define "statutory guardian" and "testamentary guardian" by direct reference to GIA ss 5, 6 and 8 and s 7, and those defined terms do the work in P.6 r 24, which is the machinery through which a PAA s 21(2) grant to an infant's guardian is actually made. This is the seam between the two Acts. The corroboration REVERSES the sweep's reading of it: the same GIA cross-reference stood in the Rules of Court O 71 r 2 for at least thirty years, so the 2024 Rules re-enact an old wiring and WIDEN it (adding AMLA Part 3 and Women's Charter Part 10 Chapter 5 limbs) rather than narrowing s 21(2); r 24(1)(a) keeps a catch-all for "any guardian appointed by a court of competent jurisdiction" and r 24(3) preserves a Registrar-assigned override, which is the procedural analogue of s 21(2)'s "or to such person as the court thinks fit". The class is corrected from binding to interpretive accordingly.

It is retained rather than dropped because it is where the encoding will diverge from practice if "guardian" is modelled as one type across both Acts: a GIA s 19 appointee — the small-estate person who takes the infant's property in "his sole and uncontrolled discretion" — is not in the Rules' qualifying class, and E38 and E39 record that "guardian" is not even uniform within the GIA.

entries.summary: PAA s 62(1) gives the Public Trustee a discretion bounded only by two statutory conditions — property not exceeding $50,000, and no pending application for letters of administration. The Public Trustee publishes eleven circumstances in which it will not act; the corroboration counts them precisely: one restates the $50,000/DPS threshold, one restates the pending-application condition while widening it to grants of probate, and NINE have no statutory footing in s 62 at all. Among the nine is an exclusion directly on this corpus's subject — the office will not act where the deceased was the sole lessee of an HDB flat and a child is eligible to inherit. The page was reworded from "We cannot act if" to "We do not act if", moving from an assertion of legal incapacity to a description of practice.

NB the page's own cross-reference "Sections 49L and 49M of the Insurance Act" is stale: the current Insurance Act 1966 numbers the nomination provisions ss 132-133.

In these cases, you will need to apply to the court for Letters of Administration to deal with the person’s estate.

entries.summary: GIA s 5A(7) reads as a live rule prescribing a Criminal Procedure Code summons route, but only "Unless the Family Justice Rules provide otherwise" — and Family Justice (General) Rules 2024 Part 3A does provide otherwise. This entry also carries the sweep's second, overlapping finding on the same displacement, and the corroboration narrows both: the displacement covers FOUR of the five application types Part 3A routes — the access enforcement application itself (r 2(2)), the respondent's and the surety's applications to discharge a compliance bond (rr 8(3), 9(3)) and the application to forfeit one (r 10(2)) — while r 7 is routed to Part 5 without a "despite section 5A(7)" rider. And the CPC is NOT evicted: r 13 expressly applies CPC ss 3, 115, 116, 119 and 120 to summonsing and Part 6 Divisions 2, 3 and 5 to warrants of arrest, which is s 5A(7)(b)(ii) being exercised rather than displaced. Precisely: s 5A(7)(a) is displaced for four application types; s 5A(7)(b)(ii) is operated by r 13. Part 3A commenced on 2 January 2025, the same day s 5A(7) itself commenced, so s 5A(7)(a) has never operated as printed.

entries.summary: Part 3A of the Family Justice (General) Rules 2024 supplies the entire operating machinery for GIA s 5A, none of which appears in s 5A itself: how the application is made, the supporting affidavit, the consequences of failing to file or to appear, the mandatory show-cause direction, variation of final orders, discharge and forfeiture of compliance bonds, and the CPC summons and warrant provisions. Two rules bind the s 5A power directly — r 5(2) requires the respondent to attend in person before a fine or imprisonment can be imposed under s 5A(3)(e), a hard precondition with no counterpart in the Act, and r 6(1) requires a show-cause direction on prima facie proof of breach. The compliance bond in s 5A(3)(d) acquires a life-cycle the Act never describes, ending in a judgment debt in favour of the Government for any unsatisfied balance.

entries.summary: The Registrar has directed that a GIA s 5A(2) access-enforcement application filed on or after 2 January 2025 in proceedings commenced BEFORE that date goes by originating application, not as a summons in the existing proceedings — the mode Row C otherwise imposes on enforcement applications in legacy proceedings, and from which Row C expressly carves this application out. The corroboration corrects the class from binding to interpretive: the direction does not change what s 5A(2) does; it confirms for legacy proceedings the filing mode the Rules already impose. entries.summary: GIA s 5 says nothing about Muslim law — GIA1934.txt was grepped for "Muslim" and returns zero hits, as do WA1838 and PAA1934 — and the gate is entirely external. SCJA 1969 s 17A(2)(b) preserves the civil court's custody jurisdiction over Muslim parties, and s 17A(3) then compels a stay in both directions, absent the appropriate Syariah Court certificate; AMLA 1966 s 35A correspondingly requires the Syariah Court's permission to commence or continue. Neither gate is absolute: both are disapplied where the parties consent and file certificates of attendance after counselling. The corroboration is strict about what the case decides — it is a PROPERTY case under s 17A(2)(c), the stay was refused, and its bearing on custody is confined to the holding that the (3)(b) limb is custody-only. It also flags an unresolved point: s 17A(3) addresses the "General Division" while GIA s 2 defines "court" as the General Division OR a Family Court, so the forum reach of the SCJA stay over a Family Court GIA application is unsettled.

entries.summary: GIA s 5 is an enabling provision for orders on custody, access and maintenance; it is NOT a power to appoint a guardian. Only two provisions expressly empower the COURT to appoint one — s 6 (s 6(1) and 6(2), appointing a guardian to act jointly with a surviving parent; s 6(3), where the infant has no parent) and s 10 (appointing a replacement on removal). The corroboration corrects the sweep on both flanks: s 7 is NOT a court appointment power — it lets a PARENT appoint a testamentary guardian taking effect only on that parent's death, with s 7(4) merely letting the court adjust an appointment already made — and the s 6 power is not confined to sub-section (3). Beyond the Act, the court may appoint under its inherent wardship jurisdiction where necessary for the child's protection, so the GIA is not exhaustive of the court's powers over infants.

[32] It appears that there is no provision in the GIA for the appointment of a guardian outside of the circumstances in ss 6, 7 and 10. Thus, court intervention for the appointment of a guardian is warranted only where there is no parent (see s 6(3) of the GIA) or in replacing a guardian (see s 10 of the GIA). ... [37] I am of the view that s 5 of our GIA does not empower the courts to appoint guardians outside of the circumstances in ss 6 and 10. ... entries.summary: "Guardian" in GIA s 10 does not include a parent, so the removal power cannot be used against a natural parent — despite ss 6(1) and 6(2) literally denominating a surviving parent "guardian of the infant". The court reached this by purposive construction: ss 6(1)-(2) were enacted in 1965 to entrench equal parental responsibility, not to equate parents with guardians, and the UK analogue permitted removal only of a testamentary or statutorily-appointed guardian. UMF v UMG had stated the proposition but expressly left it undecided; VET v VEU decides it. An unfit parent, though not removable under s 10, may still lose custody and care and control.

entries.summary: GIA s 5 imposes a standing requirement: only a parent or a guardian appointed under the Act may apply for custody, access or maintenance. A long-term de facto carer has none — here the child's grand-aunt, who had cared for him since he was seven days old. The decision departs from Lim Kok Chye Ivan v Lim Chin Huat Francis, which had held s 5 was NOT an enabling provision. The corroboration corrects one overstatement: the grandparent limb rests not on this case's facts but on its endorsement at [32] of CZ v DA. Note the asymmetry with the adjacent section: s 6(3) speaks of "the application of any person" and so is open, while s 5 is closed.

The Plaintiff, being neither, had no locus standi to apply under that provision.

entries.disposition_note: SCOPED OUT: standing to bring a custody application is the GIA's custody leg, which this corpus does not model. The statutory reform for non-parent standing urged at [69]-[70] remains unenacted.

entries.summary: The GIA uses "custody" and "the right of access" as undefined primitives, and the Court of Appeal supplied the definitions the Act lacks: residual custody is long-term decision-making, care and control is day-to-day decision-making and who the child lives with; religion, education and major healthcare fall on the custody side, dress, food and travel-to-school on the other. It also held that joint or no custody orders are the norm and sole custody the exception, and that a "no custody order" is not a deprivation of custody but a reversion to the general law of parenthood — so the order space has three states, not two. Affirmed by a later Court of Appeal in ZO v ZP ("We could not agree more") and applied as recently as May 2026.

provenance.source: Court of Appeal

provenance.quote: We believe that, generally, joint or no custody orders should be made, with sole custody orders being an exception to the rule. ... The GIA is silent as to the definition of "custody orders" ... residual "custody" is the package of residual rights that remains after the grant of a care and control order that dictates which parent shall be the daily caregiver of the child and with whom the child shall live. To put it simplistically, "care and control" concerns day-to-day decision-making, while residual "custody" concerns the long-term decision-making for the welfare of the child.

entries.summary: The Court of Appeal endorsed a five-factor, non-exhaustive welfare framework taken from the Family Law Review Working Group's 2016 Guardianship Report — the child's needs and safety; each parent's capacity; the child's relationships; continuity with both parents; the effect of change — while refusing to make it a checklist: relevance and weight are both case-dependent. Two precision points from the corroboration. The framework is not GIA-exclusive: it attaches to the welfare principle, which lives in both GIA s 3 and Women's Charter s 125(2). And it must not be conflated with GIA s 11 "Matters to be considered", which WAS amended in 2024 (E5) and carries a different, narrower statutory list.

provenance.quote: In our judgment, the factors identified in the Guardianship Report afford a sound starting basis for any court concerned with the issue of the child’s welfare. It suffices to observe that factors (a) and (b) are closely related and should generally be considered in tandem. Further, the relevance of these or any other factors to a particular case, and the weight that should be given to each of the factors, is a matter of judgment and will turn on the specific facts and circumstances of that case.

entries.summary: Considerations of comity do not override the welfare principle in guardianship and custody applications outside the International Child Abduction Act, and GIA s 3 continues to apply in all child-related custody disputes not brought under the Hague Convention. The Appellate Division respectfully departed from the judge below, who had said comity had "immense force ... and on that basis alone, the appeal ought to be dismissed". Subsisting foreign custody orders and a wrongful removal are relevant, but as facts bearing on welfare, never as an independent ground that displaces the s 3 inquiry. Qualification the corroboration insists on: s 3 applying does not entail a full merits inquiry — the court may order a child's immediate return to a foreign jurisdiction without investigating the merits. Vehicle: a dismissed permission-to-appeal application, so the passage carries the weight of a considered appellate statement rather than a holding.

provenance.quote: This is because s 3 of the GIA is generally applicable and continues to apply in all child-related custody disputes that are not brought under the Hague Convention. ... That said, in appropriate circumstances, depending on the precise facts and circumstances of the case, the court may, pursuant to the welfare principle, order the immediate return of a child to a foreign jurisdiction without conducting a full investigation of the merits ... In short, considerations of comity do not override the welfare principle in guardianship and custody applications outside the ICAA.

entries.summary: The ss 6-8 framework governing testamentary guardians applies equally, absent express provision to the contrary, to a guardian appointed during the parents' lifetime, and s 8 is not on its terms confined to cases where a parent has died. s 8's trigger is persons who "act as joint guardians", not persons formally "appointed as joint guardians" — a predicate an encoding would naturally get backwards by keying on the appointment event rather than the factual role. The corroboration is emphatic that the extension is self-limited: no s 8 application was before the court, the operative holding runs through s 5, and the judge confined the decision to the guardian before him, reserving other classes of party "to be decided when such cases arise". The s 8 construction is strictly obiter, and it should be read alongside VET v VEU (E38), decided eight weeks later without citing it, which reads the appointment powers more narrowly.

entries.summary: A GIA s 5 order made in contemplation of divorce has only interim effect and does not fetter the ancillary-matters court, which may remake it. s 5 gives the court power to "alter, vary or discharge such order" only "on the application of either parent or of any guardian appointed under this Act", which reads as the exclusive route to disturbing a GIA order; it is not. Three weight caveats from the corroboration: the Appellate Division's endorsement is obiter (the appeal concerned backdating spousal maintenance); ATZ itself followed the wife's counsel withdrawing the res judicata point, so the contrary case was conceded rather than argued; and while the language is general enough to reach s 5 maintenance orders, the framing is as to custody, care and control and access.
